misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Because an index cannot be physically delivered, index options trigger cash settlement based entirely on the net difference between the strike and index settlement value (SET) ([fact-01]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: As Hull proves in Business Snapshot 15.1, long-term put protection remains surprisingly expensive because volatility uncertainty sigma * sqrt(T) continues growing with horizon length T ([fact-10]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Net trading profit must account for the time value of money by compounding the initial premium paid at the risk-free rate: Profit = Payoff - Premium paid * e^(r*T) ([fact-11]).

activeRecallQuiz.scenario: A portfolio manager manages an equity portfolio valued at $10,000,000 with a portfolio beta of beta = 1.5. The S&P 500 index level is I = 4,000. Separately, a European call on British pounds has spot S0 = 1.6000 USD, strike K = 1.6000 USD, r = 6%, rf = 8%, sigma = 15%, T = 1 year.
activeRecallQuiz.question: 1) How many index put contracts are required to hedge the portfolio? 2) What is the economic rationale for replacing continuous dividend q with foreign rate rf in currency options?
activeRecallQuiz.correctAnswer: Correctly identifying the downside risk and margin constraints.
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Detailed pedagogical explanation grounded in source principles.

coreTakeaways: Index options feature $100 multipliers and settle in cash against index settlement value (SET) without physical delivery ([fact-01]).
Continuous dividend yields q and foreign risk-free rates rf adjust BSM pricing by replacing S0 with prepaid forward values S0 * e^(-q*T) ([fact-02], [fact-08]).
Portfolio insurance requires beta-adjusted contract sizing (N = beta * (P / (100 * I))) and proper compounding of option premiums to calculate true net trading profit ([fact-07], [fact-11]).
